summary:
Niger criminalises same-sex conduct and transition itself. Article 25 of the Charter of Refoundation, adopted by the military junta in March 2025, bans “LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior” for the five-year transition that followed the July 2023 coup. It was the first explicit prohibition of its kind at statutory level in the country, and it set no penalty of its own. The February 2026 revision of the penal code supplies the penalties; the Agence Nigérienne de Presse reported the criminalisation of LGBTQIA+ practice on 1 June 2026.

Article 390 punishes “indecent, unnatural, and LGBTQIA+ acts” with five to ten years’ imprisonment and fines of up to 100 million CFA francs. The same article reaches public announcement of a same-sex relationship and anyone who changes or attempts to change their birth sex, which places transition-related medical and legal steps inside the criminal provision. Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences are not available under the article.

Article 391 punishes same-sex marriage with ten to twenty years. Article 392 punishes creating, managing, financing or participating in LGBTQIA+ organisations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, with ten to twenty years in prison and fines of up to 500 million CFA francs, about €762,244 or US$882,829.

The drafting reaches past same-sex conduct. The Oxford Human Rights Hub states that Article 390 also criminalises a person who “artificially changes sex at birth”, which places intersex people inside the provision, and El Espectador reports that the code’s broad and confused wording reads asexuality as sanctionable conduct as well.

Enforcement under the 2026 code is documented. The Guardian reported on 1 July 2026 that at least 40 people had been arrested for homosexuality and that 16 men, including high-ranking military officials, had been imprisoned following the penal code revision, with campaigners describing a witch-hunt; local media reported dozens of arrests across the country. A trans visitor in what Niger’s law would class as a a same-sex relationship, or whose documents or presentation are read against their birth sex, faces these provisions.

Before the explicit ban, same-sex conduct was pursued through public-indecency provisions and acquittals drew reprisals against the judges who granted them. In Maradi in 2022 two young women were prosecuted over lesbianism and acquitted because no legislation then criminalised the conduct; they were nevertheless imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos allegedly portraying a lesbian act, and the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after the acquittal. In Niamey in 2025 two young women were prosecuted for public indecency and acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere, and the judge was allegedly sanctioned for being too lenient.

Care access has contracted alongside the ban. Organisations providing HIV prevention services to men who have sex with men stopped working after the 2026 law, and a representative warned that people no longer have access to condoms, HIV testing or PrEP; campaigners told The Guardian they fear an HIV resurgence as access to PrEP collapses.

Niger has no broad legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The only other statutory protection, Article 4 of Law 2015-36 on Illicit Trafficking of Migrants, was repealed in 2023 by decree of President Abdourahamane Tiani, which also expunged prior convictions and their effects.

Official positions are hostile. Justice Minister Alio Daouda said that “all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be” are “not in line with our social and cultural values”, and public debate around President Mohamed Bazoum’s 2023 proposals was framed in terms of “social contagion”. After the 2026 law LGBTQ people went into hiding, and Niger’s authorities refused to recognise the refugee status of the people who staged the country’s first LGBTQ public demonstration in Niamey in 2022.
tangentialFactors:
The legislative path to the current code ran through parliamentary motion and draft legislation. In December 2022 lawmakers backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships, moved by MP Nana Djibou Harouna of the southern Maradi region, weeks after a Maradi court acquitted two young women of lesbianism charges because no legislation criminalised same-sex relationships. A 2023 draft penal code proposed up to five years for same-sex conduct, 20 years for conducting, officiating or witnessing a same-sex marriage, and five years for participating in or financing “homosexual” organisations; the February 2026 code set the marriage and organisation penalties at ten to twenty years.

The age of consent has been unequal by partner sex: 13 for different-sex acts against 21 for same-sex acts. Outright International reports that the code fixes the ages at 21 and 13 respectively, while Wikipedia dates the same disparity to the pre-2025 rules.

El Espectador places the February 2026 code within a wave of African states hardening their anti-LGBTQIA+ laws. The announcement itself came through the state news agency on 1 June 2026, and Justice Minister Alio Daouda’s public framing of the policy is on record.

The most recent documentary assessment of violence in this inventory is the U.S. State Department’s 2013 Human Rights Report, which found no reports of violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity and no documented cases of discrimination, while cautioning that stigma and intimidation probably kept incidents unreported. The same report recorded two men caught naked in a parked car arrested and fined for public indecency, and no documented cases of discrimination in education.

Two gay rights organisations reportedly operated in secret in Niger, partly because they were not formally registered, before the 2026 law took effect.
localsOnly:
Article 95 of Law 2022-59 on the Protection of Personal Data prohibits collecting or processing data that reveals sexual orientation, punishable by three months to five years’ imprisonment and fines of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs. The law was published by the Ministry of Communication and New Information Technologies in June 2025.

Article 392 of the 2026 penal code applies to organisations directly: creating, managing, financing or participating in LGBTQIA+ organisations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, carries ten to twenty years in prison and fines up to 500 million CFA francs. After the law, the organisations providing HIV prevention services to men who have sex with men stopped working, and residents lost access to condoms, HIV testing and PrEP through those channels.

LGBTQIA people in Niger face stigmatisation among the broader population. Since the 2026 law, LGBTQ people have gone into hiding; historically many led socially acceptable public lives while keeping relationships private.

Niger offers residents no broad legal protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and the 2023 decree repealing Article 4 of Law 2015-36 also expunged prior convictions and their effects.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry, visa and passport gender-marker rules for Niger are not sourced in this inventory; whether Nigerian border or consular screening flags document markers or gender presentation is unresolved here.

Whether Articles 390 to 392 apply to foreign visitors as distinct from residents, and whether gender-affirming medical steps taken by a visitor fall inside Article 390, is not stated in these sources.

The dating of the unequal age of consent is unresolved: Outright International attaches the 21-versus-13 split to “the code”, while Wikipedia dates it to the pre-2025 rules.

Article 25 of the Charter of Refoundation set no penalty of its own; whether that article remains in force alongside the February 2026 penal code is not stated in these sources.

No trans-specific killing or violence figure with a denominator appears in this inventory. The Guardian’s “at least 40” arrests and 16 imprisonments (1 July 2026) and the “dozens” reported by local media are raw counts without a population denominator and are not ranked against other jurisdictions here; no comparison to Niger’s general homicide rate is available, so no trans-specific rate can be stated.

Figures distinguishing arrests of trans people from those of cisgender gay and bisexual men are not available; the documented enforcement counts group all people charged with homosexuality together.

Facilities, bathroom access and hospital or clinic capacity for trans-specific care inside Niger are not documented in these sources.
